surfaces.part: middle and left rock stone faces

answer.evidence: Three snow-capped rocks sit on a white snow drift. At x=8 the snow cap covers rows 5-7, then dark rows 8-9 act as eave shadow above the gray stone face (rows 8-10), so the left rock shows a top band with an edge line. The middle rock's cap is thinner: snow on rows 3-4 at x=15, then a stone face on rows 5-9. A dark base line at row 10 separates the rocks from the snow bank (rows 11-14). The tops are small and sloped but present, and each rock has a front face of 3+ rows. The reading is a marginal three_quarter because the caps are only about 2-3 rows thick.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a tiny grey rock-and-snow cluster, not a tree. It is far smaller than the references and has no canopy or trunk, so the kind does not match and the references cannot be compared fairly. By eye it shows only about 3 grey ramp steps with a dark neutral outline. The measured facts agree on the outline: 100% of dark edge pixels are near-neutral, against 0% for both references, which is the sticker look. The 16 visible tones are a misleading figure for a piece this small. By eye it has no clumped foliage, bark grain or per-element shading like the references. It is clearly flatter and thinner than the references, and it is the wrong kind of object, so it fails.

answer.evidence: The tallest rock (x=15) has a snow tip at rows 3-4, then a flat grey face at rows 5-9 and a dark base line at row 10. The width grows steadily from 1 to 25 over rows 2-10, so the silhouette is a dome with no widen-then-narrow ellipse. The snow on the left rock (rows 5-7) and middle rock (rows 3-4) is a thin cap of 1-3 rows with no front-edge line or eave shadow, so it reads as a rim or hat rather than a top plane. The rock faces are vertical and shaded. The white snow band at rows 11-14 is a flat ground strip, not a top surface of the rocks. This is a front elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a tiny grey rock cluster sitting on a white base, not a tree, bush or other plant. It has no canopy or trunk, so it does not match the reference kind. It is about 1-2 tiles wide and shows only about 3 grey steps on the stones. The 16 visible tones per tile in the measured facts come mostly from antialiased edges and the white base, not from real shading depth. 100% of its dark edge pixels are near-neutral, which indicates a neutral dark outline and a sticker look, whereas both references have 0%. The references have large clustered canopies with 5-6 greens and tinted outlines. Against them the candidate is far smaller, flatter and thinner, with no leaf clumps or grain. Overall it would look much weaker next to the references.

surfaces.part: snow drift base under the rocks

answer.evidence: Three grey boulders stand on a white snow base. The largest, in the middle, has only a 2-row snow cap (rows 3-4) on a 5-row grey face (rows 5-9). Its right side is darker, which reads as a receding side face. The left rock has a 3-row snow cap (rows 5-7) with 2 rows of shadow below it. A dark line at row 10 separates the rocks from the 4-row white base (rows 11-14). The rock tops are only thin, rim-like snow patches, not a real horizontal surface, so the main body reads mostly as a front elevation. The wide white base could be read as a flat drift, but it is ground rather than the rocks' own top.

The dark edge pixels are 100% near-neutral, against 0% in both references, which points to a neutral dark outline with no material tint. It is far thinner and flatter than either reference, which have rich multi-tone canopies, so a careful artist would not accept it next to them.

answer.evidence: Three rounded rock heads sit on a white snow drift. The middle rock is the largest, and column x=15 shows only a 1-2 row snow highlight (rows 3-4) before the gray face runs rows 5-9. The left rock has a 3-row snow cap (rows 5-7) but no front-edge line or eave shadow, and its face is drawn straight below as a vertical gray block. The dark line at row 10 separates the rocks from the snow base. The base (rows 11-15) is a flat white band with a shaded bottom row and no ellipse or edge line. No rock shows a distinct horizontal top plane, so the drawing reads as a front elevation.
